p|bad|at.sig: I'm terrible at remembering names, and bad ___ maths too.#at#in/on/to/of/with/about

en.why: *bad* uses *at* to indicate lack of skill in a particular area.

wrong.in: "bad in" is not the correct collocation for ability.
wrong.of: "bad of" is not used for competence.

p|good|at.sig: My brother is really good ___ maths.#at#in/on/of/about/from/by

en.why: *good* uses *at* to talk about skill in a subject or activity.

wrong.in: "good in" is not the standard collocation for skill.

p|good|for.sig: Walking every day is good ___ your heart.#for#in/on/of/about/from/by

en.why: *for* indicates that something is beneficial or useful to someone or something.

wrong.on: "good on" is not used for usefulness.

p|good|to.sig: My neighbours have always been good ___ me.#to#in/on/of/about/from/by

en.why: *to* expresses kindness or favorable treatment toward a person.

wrong.on: "good on" is not used for people.
wrong.of: "good of" changes meaning to moral quality.

en.why: *with* shows ability to handle or interact well with someone or something.

wrong.in: "good in" does not express handling ability.
wrong.on: "good on" is not used for interaction.
wrong.by: "good by" does not convey dealing ability.

p|interested|in.sig: She has always been interested ___ marine biology.#in#on/at/for/to/of/with

en.why: *interested* always takes *in* to express curiosity about something.

wrong.at: "interested at" would refer to a location, not curiosity.
wrong.to: "interested to" is used with infinitives, not nouns.
wrong.with: "interested with" changes the meaning and is uncommon.
